en.title: Hafjell snow by month: when Norway's family mountain is at its best
en.description: Hafjell above Lillehammer month by month: usual snow depth at the base, mid-mountain and the top from 46 past winters, the first snow, the deepest weeks and how the recent winters compare.
en.lede: Hafjell is the big, gentle mountain above Lillehammer: 39 km of mapped runs served by 17 lifts, from the valley at 192 m to the top at 1058 m. It is not high by Alpine standards, so the question families ask is simple: when is there enough snow, and when is it at its best? Our snow history of 46 past winters answers it height by height.

sections.h: The first snow comes in October, the skiing in December
p: At mid-mountain (625 m) the first snow of the winter has arrived by October 19 in half of the past winters, and by October 30 even at the base. That first snow rarely lasts. The usual depth in November is only 20 cm at mid-mountain, with a wide spread from 3 to 47 cm between a poor and a rich November.

December is when the mountain turns white for good: 50 cm at mid-mountain and 60 cm at the top in a typical year. Hafjell makes a lot of snow on its lower runs, and the cold Gudbrandsdalen air keeps it, which is why the resort can open its main runs before the natural cover alone would allow.

sections.h: January to March: the deep months
p: The depth keeps climbing through the winter. January brings 78 cm at mid-mountain, February 88 cm and March 91 cm, which is the deepest month of a usual winter at every height. At the top the March figure is 101 cm.

The best single week at mid-mountain is ISO week 11, in the first half of March, when 100 per cent of the past winters had at least 50 cm there and the usual depth was 92 cm. For a trip you book months ahead, late February and March are the safest dates.

sections.h: How reliable is it? Weeks with real snow
p: We count the weeks in which mid-mountain had at least 50 cm of snow. Hafjell reaches that in 12 weeks in nine of ten winters, and in 20 weeks in half of them. The top does better: 15 weeks in nine of ten winters.
The winter peak at mid-mountain is 106 cm in a typical year, between 73 cm in the poorest past winter and 159 cm in the richest. Last winter peaked at 85 cm there, below the usual.

sections.h: April: spring skiing on the upper mountain
p: Snow lasts long on this mountain. At the top the usual depth in April is still 99 cm, and the last snow of the winter at mid-mountain is gone by May 22 in half of the past winters. The base melts out earlier, so spring trips are a top-half affair.

sections.h: Month by month at three heights
p: In December a usual winter has 40 cm at the base (192 m), 50 cm at mid-mountain (625 m) and 60 cm at the top (1058 m). In January a usual winter has 69 cm at the base (192 m), 78 cm at mid-mountain (625 m) and 86 cm at the top (1058 m). In February a usual winter has 79 cm at the base (192 m), 88 cm at mid-mountain (625 m) and 96 cm at the top (1058 m).

In March a usual winter has 81 cm at the base (192 m), 91 cm at mid-mountain (625 m) and 101 cm at the top (1058 m). In April a usual winter has 60 cm at the base (192 m), 78 cm at mid-mountain (625 m) and 99 cm at the top (1058 m).

sections.h: A poor winter and a rich winter
p: The spread matters as much as the middle. At mid-mountain, nine of ten past Marchs had at least 65 cm and one in ten had 126 cm or more; at the top the same range runs from 72 to 139 cm.

Over the whole winter the peak at mid-mountain ran from 73 cm in the poorest past winter to 159 cm in the richest, around a usual 106 cm; at the top from 73 to 191 cm around 119 cm. Snow lay on the ground at mid-mountain for 205 days in a usual winter, and the first snow of the season settled there by October 19 in half of the winters. These are model values for the area over 46 past winters, not resort measurements; they describe what to expect, not what the groomers will add.

Comparing the first 15 of our 46 winters with the last 15, the peak at the top went from 122 cm to 118 cm, a small change. The number of days with snow on the ground at mid-mountain fell from 213 to 194: the depth holds, the season is a little shorter at both ends.

advice: Book February or March for the deepest and most reliable snow at every height.
December works thanks to snowmaking and cold air; expect natural cover mainly on the upper half.
Snow on our map does not mean a lift is open: check the resort's own lift status before you travel.
For a car-free trip, the mountain is a short bus ride from Lillehammer station.
